title: ⭐⭐ Practice: back on yourself, and told what to do

questions.prompt: Emna is checking four sentences she has written in her English notebook. Three of them are correct. In which one has she put a reflexive pronoun where English uses none at all?

options.text: Rania hurt herself on the corner of the desk.
Mouna taught herself to use the new program.
Khaled felt himself very tired after the last paper.
The two candidates introduced themselves to the examiner.

questions.explanation: "Khaled felt himself very tired after the last paper." is the sentence to correct: in English the verb feel followed by an adjective takes no pronoun at all, and the line should read Khaled felt very tired. Your own language builds this verb with a pronoun, and that is exactly why the mistake is so common. "Rania hurt herself on the corner of the desk." is correct, and the reflexive is compulsory there: Rania is the one who hurts and the one who is hurt. "Mouna taught herself to use the new program." is correct too, and means that she had no teacher, the reflexive filling the place of the person taught. And "The two candidates introduced themselves to the examiner." is correct as well: they gave their own names, so the doer and the receiver are once again the same people.

questions.prompt: A revision leaflet handed out in a school in Gafsa carries this line: "Do not leave the exam room before the end of the time." Nizar has to give the same advice again, this time with had better. Which version is correct English?

options.text: You had better not leave the room before the end of the time.
You hadn't better leave the room before the end of the time.
You had better not to leave the room before the end of the time.
You had better don't leave the room before the end of the time.

questions.explanation: "You had better not leave the room before the end of the time." is right: had better is made negative by putting not straight after better, and the verb that follows stays bare, with no to in front of it. "You hadn't better leave the room before the end of the time." treats had as an ordinary auxiliary and contracts the negative onto it, which this expression never allows; the not belongs after better. "You had better not to leave the room before the end of the time." adds a to that had better never takes, unlike ought to, which keeps its own. And "You had better don't leave the room before the end of the time." builds a second negative with do inside a sentence that already has its modal; a modal is never followed by don't.

questions.prompt: Mouna is sorting the new words of the theme into two columns. Three of these four name something that happens to a candidate in an exam room. The fourth names something one person does to another. Which one is the fourth?

options.text: to panic
to fail
to go blank
to suppress

questions.explanation: "to suppress" is the odd one: it means to put an end to something, and it needs somebody who does it and something that is done away with, which is why the uniform file uses it of the schools that suppress the individuality of their pupils. Nothing suppresses a candidate; a candidate suppresses something. "to panic" names a state that comes over a person, and nobody panics somebody else. "to fail" is what happens to a candidate who does not reach the mark, and it describes the result of one person's paper, not an action aimed at another person. And "to go blank" is said of a mind that suddenly holds nothing at all, which is again something the candidate undergoes rather than something anybody does.

questions.prompt: In three of these four sentences the reflexive pronoun can be crossed out and the sentence goes on saying exactly the same thing. In which one would crossing it out leave a sentence with a hole in it?

options.text: The pupils painted the club room themselves.
Rania cut herself on a sheet of paper.
The head teacher herself opened the meeting.
We carried the boxes upstairs ourselves.

questions.explanation: "Rania cut herself on a sheet of paper." is the sentence that would break: herself is the object of cut, and it names the person the cutting was done to. Take it away and Rania cut on a sheet of paper no longer says what she cut, so the reflexive there is compulsory. In "The pupils painted the club room themselves." the object is already the club room, and themselves only insists that no painter was called in; The pupils painted the club room is still a full and true sentence. "The head teacher herself opened the meeting." shows the same emphatic use in another position, right after the subject, and it can be removed just as easily. And "We carried the boxes upstairs ourselves." again has its object, the boxes, so ourselves adds emphasis and nothing more.

questions.prompt: A candidate always finishes her paper twenty minutes before the end and hands it in at once. Three of these four sentences give her advice that fits her problem. Which one gives her the opposite advice?

options.text: You had better use every minute you are given, right to the end.
You ought to read all your answers again before you hand the paper in.
You needn't leave the room the moment you have written your last line.
You had better hand your paper in the moment you have finished.

questions.explanation: "You had better hand your paper in the moment you have finished." is the odd one: it tells the candidate to keep doing exactly what is costing her marks, and it puts a warning behind that instruction, as if leaving early were the safe choice. "You had better use every minute you are given, right to the end." warns her against the very habit described, which is the advice she needs. "You ought to read all your answers again before you hand the paper in." says the same thing in the language of duty, and gives her something useful to do with the twenty minutes. And "You needn't leave the room the moment you have written your last line." frees her from a rule she has invented for herself, since nothing obliges a candidate to hand in a paper early.

questions.prompt: Emna is copying the useful expressions of the theme onto the last page of her notebook. Three of her four lines are correct English. Which line must she cross out and write again?

options.text: to cope with the pressure of the last week
to conform to the rules of the school
to fail in the written exam
to check your answers twice

questions.explanation: "to fail in the written exam" is the line to cross out: when its object is an exam, a test or a subject, the verb fail takes that object straight, with no preposition between them, so Emna must write to fail the written exam. The extra in is copied from her own language and is one of the errors most often seen on a paper. "to cope with the pressure of the last week" is right, and cope never loses its with; a candidate copes with stress, never copes stress. "to conform to the rules of the school" is right too, and conform keeps to in the same way. And "to check your answers twice" is correct as it stands: check takes its object directly, and adding a preposition to it would break it.
